scams.name: The Gion / Pontocho Bar Tout Hostess Trap
scams.description: A well-dressed man approaches tourists on nightlife streets, offering recommendations to a bar with 'first drink free.' Victims are led upstairs where hostesses sit uninvited, drinks appear without ordering, and bouncers block exits. Final bills reach ¥60,000+ for watered whisky and undisclosed company fees. Kyoto's anti-tout ordinance (since 2015) makes street soliciting illegal citywide.
scams.avoidance: Never follow strangers into bars you didn't independently research on Google Maps or Tabelog. Anyone approaching you on Pontocho or Gion streets is breaking local law—walk past without engagement. Always request a price list before sitting ('料金表を見せてください'). If pressured, call 110 and say 'bottakuri.' Stick to street-level izakayas with clear signage, Japanese customers, and 4.2+ ratings.
scams.location: Pontocho, Kawaramachi, Kiyamachi, and Gion nightlife streets

scams.name: The Gion Private-Road ¥10,000 Fine (Geisha Photo Shakedown)
scams.description: Tourists photograph people in maiko dress on Gion side streets and either encounter a 'manager' demanding ¥1,000-5,000 or face a real ¥10,000 fine enforced since April 2024 by the Gion Machi Nan-gawa Council. The council closed narrow private alleys off Hanamikoji after repeated incidents of tourists grabbing kimono sleeves and blocking maiko appointments. Signs in four languages warn of penalties; touching a maiko is criminal assault carrying up to ¥500,000 in fines and six months in jail.
scams.avoidance: Photograph geiko and maiko only from Hanamikoji's main public road, never from side alleys with '私道・立入禁止・罰金1万円' signs. If someone demands cash for a photo, politely decline and walk toward Shijo-dori—no legal basis exists for the shakedown. Never touch, grab, or block anyone in kimono. Consider lawful geisha encounters at Gion Corner or ozashiki dinners (¥3,500-50,000) instead.
scams.location: Hanamikoji Street, Kodai-ji side alleys, and Gion's private lanes

scams.name: The Arashiyama 'Dream Cafe' Bait-and-Switch
scams.description: An older woman sweeping the pavement recruits tourists into a charming-looking café promising 'Kyoto cultural experience' for ¥3,000. Inside, guests receive odd-tasting hojicha, then staff offer 'exclusive meetings with Mr Hayakawa' for ¥63,000 per hour. Dream Cafe accumulated 1.4-star reviews before Kyoto Prefectural Police raided it on fraud charges. The touting pattern persists despite venue closure.
scams.avoidance: Never enter Arashiyama cafés or tea-ceremony venues recruited via street touting—touting itself is illegal under Kyoto City ordinance. Pre-select matcha and kaiseki venues on Google Maps (4.3+ ratings, 200+ reviews) before arrival. Watch for multilingual warning signs marking known-bad blocks. Refuse bills over ¥2,000 for tea without printed pricing and call 110. Prefer established teahouses with Tabelog profiles where Japanese and English menus match exactly.
scams.location: Arashiyama tourist street near Togetsukyo Bridge and bamboo grove approach

scams.name: The No-Menu Restaurant Near Kinkaku-ji / Kiyomizu
scams.description: Restaurants immediately adjacent to major sights display picture-only menus at the door with no prices. After customers commit to seating, prices are revealed, often inflating modest meals to ¥6,000+ per head (expected ¥1,500). Most-reported pattern on r/JapanTravel after bar touts. Venues may charge 10% service tax plus 10% consumption tax stacked together.
scams.avoidance: Always ask '料金は？' (how much?) before sitting. Walk two to three streets away from sights before choosing restaurants—value drops significantly. Check Tabelog (not Google Maps, which lists tourist-trap venues) before entering. If given only English menus, request Japanese versions; refusal signals foreigner-premium pricing. Avoid venues charging both '消費税10%' and 'サービス料10%' simultaneously.
scams.location: Streets immediately outside Kinkaku-ji, Kiyomizu-dera approach (Ninen-zaka, Sannen-zaka), and Arashiyama main drag

scams.name: The Kyoto Airbnb / Minpaku 'Pay on Arrival' Scam
scams.description: Hosts message guests after confirmation (via WhatsApp or LINE, not the platform) demanding passport scans and extra cleaning fees not listed. Alternative patterns include properties at non-existent addresses or hosts demanding cash on arrival with promised Airbnb refunds later. Off-platform payment requests violate platform policy. Unlicensed operators seek cash to avoid paper trails.
scams.avoidance: All payment and messaging must occur through booking platforms; report off-platform requests immediately to Airbnb/Booking.com. Passport checks are legally required but performed face-to-face on arrival only—never upload scans to host-provided URLs. Verify properties display minpaku license numbers (6-digit codes like M230000000) at entry and in listings. If hosts cancel last-minute, let the platform rebook you at their cost. Prefer central Kyoto hotels (Shijo, Karasuma, Kawaramachi) for first-time visitors.
scams.location: Kyoto short-term rentals booked via Airbnb, Booking.com, and third-party sites

scams.name: The Unlicensed 'White Taxi' (Shirotaku) from Kansai Airport and Kyoto Station
scams.description: Plainclothes drivers approach exhausted arrivals at Kansai Airport or Kyoto Station offering flat-rate 'taxi' rides (¥15,000 KIX-Kyoto or ¥5,000-8,000 locally). Vehicles display white license plates instead of green taxi plates. Drivers are uninsured, unlicensed, unregulated on fares, and linked to organized crime; October 2024 and January 2026 arrests involved 10 Chinese nationals operating these rings.
scams.avoidance: Use only official taxi queues at Kansai Airport and Kyoto Station (Hachijo and Karasuma exits); look for green license plates, company logos, and 空車 (available) lights. Take JR Haruka Express (¥2,900-3,600), Keihan Bus, or prebooked MK Skygate Shuttle (¥4,400) from Kansai. For Kyoto Station to Gion: metered official taxi (¥1,500-2,000) or Subway Karasuma Line (¥220). Use Japan Taxi / Go / Uber apps for licensed dispatches with photo/receipt documentation.
scams.location: Kansai International Airport arrivals, Kyoto Station Hachijo exit, and hotel pickups in central Kyoto

scams.name: The Fake Buddhist Monk Bracelet Donation
scams.description: Men in saffron or black robes place unsolicited gold-foil bracelets or cards into tourists' hands, bow deeply, then open donation registers showing names with ¥5,000-10,000 entries—implying expected matching contributions. The 'blessing' is theatre; real Japanese Buddhist monks do not solicit from strangers on streets. Pattern documented at Fushimi Inari, Kinkaku-ji, Gion, and near temples.
scams.avoidance: Keep walking and refuse anything handed to you—'No thank you' with a head shake is culturally acceptable. Donate to Kyoto temples only through fixed collection boxes (saisen-bako) inside main halls. If an item is placed in your hand, calmly return it and continue walking; no obligation exists. Real Kyoto monks wear sect-specific dark robes and travel in groups or to known locations; lone 'monks' in bright saffron on Gion streets are scammers. Alert temple staff at nearest shrine office.
scams.location: Fushimi Inari, Kinkaku-ji approach, Arashiyama, Gion, and around Kyoto Station

scams.name: Hidden Cover Charge / Otoshi Shock at Gion & Pontocho Izakayas
scams.description: A small dish of pickled vegetables appears before ordering—this is otoshi (お通し), a legitimate ¥300-800 per-person seating fee standard in Japanese izakaya culture. However, predatory tourist-zone venues inflate it to ¥2,000-3,000 per person, often combined with ¥500 oshibori fees, ¥1,000 seat charges, and 10% service taxes stacked with 10% consumption tax, tripling bills.
scams.avoidance: Before sitting ask '席料とお通しはいくらですか？' (how much are seat charge and otoshi?). Understand otoshi is normal—¥300-800 per person is standard; ¥1,000+ is predatory. Refusing politely is possible ('お通しは結構です') but some venues refuse seating. Check Tabelog where otoshi prices appear in reviews. Demand itemised receipts (領収書) before paying—a legal right. Look for Tabelog 3.5+ ratings explicitly noting 'no table charge' or chains like Torikizoku with all-inclusive pricing.
scams.location: Gion, Pontocho, Kiyamachi and Kawaramachi izakayas and small bars
